To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the choice of method has a substantial impact on the results; (2) the choice of time period has a strong impact on the results, with a strong tendency towards lower contributions for more recent periods; (3) the choice of the time period has a stronger impact than the choice of the method; and (4) the choice of a time period is strongly related to the choice of the reference period for calculating contributions.

the results depend on choices of the time period, the baseline, the emissions data, the emissions sources, and the attribution methodology, and that the choice of the baseline has the largest influence on calculated contributions.

(1) historical emissions are not the most important determinant of countries' contributions to global warming, (2) the ranking of countries' contributions varies with methodological choices, and (3) the choice of methodology has substantial effects on the size of contributions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the historical contributions to climate change can be calculated and how this information can be used in the political process.
the question of what constitutes a fair distribution of efforts in the context of climate change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

historical contributions to global mean surface temperature (GMST) change are not an appropriate measure for assessing countries' contributions to global warming and climate change, but that they can be used as one element in a broader analysis of responsibility.
there is no conclusive answer to the question how much each country contributed to global warming.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the more one wants to attribute historical responsibility for climate change to a particular nation, the more one must assume that the climate system is sensitive to anthropogenic emissions, the more one assumes that climate change is caused by CO2 emissions, and the more one assumes the climate system is linear.
there is no simple answer to how much countries have contributed to global warming.
historical contributions to climate change are a complex and multifaceted issue, and that there is not one single answer to this question.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of methodological assumptions has a strong effect, not only on the rank order of countries' contributions, but also on the absolute magnitude of calculated contributions.
the choice of methodological approach has a strong effect in determining which countries are identified as having contributed most to global warming.
the choice of the methodological framework has strong effects on the results, and thus that the methodological framework is a key determinant of the outcomes.
